questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Proto-Industrialisation' refers to.
questions.a: Proto-industrialisation refers to the phase before factories, when production was carried out in the countryside through networks of merchant-capitalists who supplied raw materials to rural households.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Proto-Industrialisation'.
questions.a: Even before factories, a system of rural, household-based production for distant markets existed, laying the groundwork for factories.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Proto-Industrialisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Before the Factory

concepts.title: The Coming Up of the Factory

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Coming Up of the Factory' refers to.
questions.a: Factories emerged in the late eighteenth century as a new form of production where workers and machinery were concentrated under one roof, allowing closer supervision and control over labour.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Coming Up of the Factory'.
questions.a: The factory concentrated production and labour under one roof, increasing control, efficiency and output.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Coming Up of the Factory' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Coming Up of the Factory

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Pace of Industrial Change' refers to.
questions.a: Industrialisation was gradual; new technology spread slowly, and traditional forms of production coexisted with factories for a long time because old methods remained profitable and flexible.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Pace of Industrial Change'.
questions.a: Industrialisation was not rapid or uniform; new and old technologies coexisted because old methods still served many markets.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Pace of Industrial Change' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Pace of Industrial Change

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Life of the Workers' refers to.
questions.a: Workers' lives were marked by uncertain employment, low wages, long hours and periods of unemployment; labour was abundant and fear of job loss kept wages low.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Life of the Workers'.
questions.a: The abundance of labour and fear of unemployment gave workers little bargaining power, making their lives insecure.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Life of the Workers' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Life of the Workers

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Industrialisation in the Colonies' refers to.
questions.a: In colonies like India, industrialisation was shaped by colonial rule: British policies favoured the import of British manufactures and the export of Indian raw materials, while Indian businessmen later set up their own factories.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Industrialisation in the Colonies'.
questions.a: Colonial industrialisation was constrained by British economic policies, but Indian entrepreneurs eventually established factories.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Industrialisation in the Colonies' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Industrialisation in the Colonies

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Market for Goods' refers to.
questions.a: Creating a market for manufactured goods required advertising, branding and persuasion; consumers had to be convinced to buy factory-made products over hand-made ones.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Market for Goods'.
questions.a: Demand for factory goods had to be actively created through marketing, brands and advertising.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Market for Goods' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Market for Goods

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Workers' Struggles' refers to.
questions.a: Workers organised strikes and protests to demand better wages, shorter hours and safer conditions; over time, laws were passed to regulate working conditions and limit employers' power.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Workers' Struggles'.
questions.a: Collective action by workers gradually forced improvements in wages, hours and working conditions through legislation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Workers' Struggles' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Workers' Struggles

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Handloom and the Factory' refers to.
questions.a: Handloom weaving did not disappear with factories; it survived and even expanded in some regions by adapting to new demands, using improved technology and specialising in fine cloth.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Handloom and the Factory'.
questions.a: Handloom production coexisted with factories by adapting, specialising and meeting demand for fine and varied cloth.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Handloom and the Factory' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Pace of Industrial Change
